spans.content: Applying abundance/biomass comparisons on a small
mammal assemblage from Barn owl (Tyto alba) pellets
(Mount Soratte, central Italy): a cautionary note
Simona Prete
\cdot
Corrado Battisti
\cdot
Francesca Marini •
Paolo Ciucci
Received: 2 November 2011 / Accepted: 14 May 2012 / Published online: 8 June 2012
Accademia Nazionale dei Lincei 2012
Abstract Abundance/biomass comparisons (or ABC
curves) allow to obtain information on the level of
(anthropogenic or natural) disturbance that may sensu lato
affect specific communities. In order to verify the general
validity of the ABC curves, we applied these comparisons
to a small mammal dataset obtained by a sample of Barn
owl (Tyto alba) pellets collected in a nature reserve of
central Italy (Monte Soratte). From 43 pellets, we obtained
111 individuals belonging to 11 shrews and rodents spe-
cies. Microtus savii, Apodemus sylvaticus, and Apodemus
flavicollis were the species most frequently preyed upon by
owls. Indices such as absolute (and normalized) species
richness and Shannon–Wiener diversity consistently
showed higher values than those obtained in similar studies
in central Italy, highlighting the complex structure of this
assemblage occurring in a landscape with low anthropiza-
tion. From ABC curves, abundance was slightly lower than
biomass, even though differences between paired cumula-
tive frequencies were not significant. This pattern suggests
that the small mammal community in our study area
features a low level of disturbance. Nevertheless, whereas
in undisturbed assemblages a higher biomass in ABC
curves indicate a higher frequency of larger species at
higher trophic level, in small mammal assemblages such as
those revealed by owl pellets, large-sized species are her-
bivorous, synanthropic and typical of disturbed habitats.
Accordingly, we caution that in disturbed habitats an
increase of small mammals with high body mass may
results in ABC curves with biomass higher than abundance.
Our results therefore suggest that there might be relevant
exceptions to the general patterns so far developed for
ABC curves.

1 Introduction
In community ecology, we may obtain large datasets on the
abundance and biomass of species assemblages that may be
analyzed using different approaches (e.g., Wiens 1989;
Krebs 2001; Magurran 2004). Among them, the most used
are the diversity/dominance diagrams (or Whittaker plots),
the
\mathbf { k }
-dominance plots and the abundance/biomass com-
parisons (or ABC curves; Warwick 1986; Lambshead et al.
1983; Krebs 1999; Magurran 2004). All the diagrams
obtained by these analyses explicit the frequency ratio (or
dominance) among species, either calculated on individual
abundance (e.g., diversity/dominance diagrams, and
k-dominance plots) or cumulatively, based on abundance
and biomass contemporarily (e.g., ABC curves). These
representations provide an explicit information on the
structure of species assemblages (e.g., diversity and even-
ness), but they also allow to obtain general information on

the natural or anthropogenic stress that might affect the
assemblages. For example, under Whittaker’s and k-dom-
inance plots more elevated abundance curves represent the
less diverse and more stressed assemblages, while in ABC
curves comparison between the biomass and abundance
curves is used to make inferences on the level of distur-
bance affecting the assemblages (Magurran 2004).
Terrestrial small mammals (shrews and rodents) con-
stitute a significant component of vertebrate communities,
and their monitoring allows large sets of data with a
moderate research effort. In turn, these datasets may pro-
vide information on the naturalness or, on the contrary, the
level of disturbance at a site (Avenant 2005). Indeed, small
mammal communities, for their large number of individ-
uals and species, may be largely affected from environ-
mental changes and anthropogenic or natural disturbances
(e.g., de la Pena et al. 2003).
Studies on small mammal communities utilizing owl
(Strigiformes) pellets have been widely carried out in the
last 30 years (Contoli 1976a, 1976b, 1976c, 1976d; Lovari
et al. 1976; Mikkola 1983). These studies focused on aut-
ecology of the predator (e.g., Love et al. 2000), synecology
of the species assemblage and their variations in time and
space (Aste and Contoli 1987; Aloise et al. 1990; Bont-
zorlos et al. 2005), biogeography at population and com-
munity level (e.g., Barbosa et al. 1992; Battisti et al. 1997),
and nature reserve management (e.g., Amori and Pas-
qualucci 1987; de la Pena et al. 2003). In these studies,
Barn owl (Tyto alba) is a widely utilized species because of
its wide distribution and because owl pellets are easy to
collect (Contoli 1980; Mikkola 1983).
Some authors (e.g., Mikkola 1983) believe that species’
frequencies in Barn owl pellets are proportional to the true
relative abundance of their prey. Nevertheless, evidences
from other authors (e.g., Capizzi and Luiselli 1996; Yom-
Tov and Wool 1997) suggest that prey assemblages from
owl pellets reveal different species proportions when
compared to trapping.
In this work, we report the structure of a small mam-
mal assemblage obtained by Barn owl pellets from a
nature reserve located in central Italy. In particular, we
applied ABC curves to compare abundance and biomass
obtained from this assemblage to evaluate its degree of
natural or anthropogenic disturbance. Among vertebrates,
the ABC approach has been recently applied in fish and
bird assemblages (Penczak and Kruk 1999; Magurran and
Phillip 2001; Benassi et al. 2009), but it was never
applied to a mammal assemblage. In particular, we ver-
ified if the general validity of the abundance/biomass
comparison, and its relative management implications
(i.e., disturbed vs. undisturbed assemblages) may be
extended to a small mammal assemblage as reconstructed
from owl’s pellets.
2 Materials and methods
2.1 Study area
The study area is located inside the ‘‘Monte Soratte’’ nature
reserve (hereafter, MSNR; 444.6 ha), a protected area sited

2.2 Field methods and data analysis
The research was carried out on a sample of Barn owl’s
pellets collected in December 2010 inside an abandoned
rural house named ‘‘Fornace’’

lected, owl pellets were dried in open air and subsequently
processed according to standardized techniques (Contoli
Mammal species represented inside owl pellets can be
easily identified and classified according to their skulls or
other diagnostic bones, following the keys reported in
Chaline et al. (1974), Contoli (1976d, 1983), Mikkola
(1983), Nappi (2001), Amori et al. (2008). We identified
the species using a binocular microscope at

Apodemus sp. were classified by a specialist (G. Amori,

To estimate the proportions of species in the small
mammal community using prey proportions as revealed in
owl pellets, we assumed that: (1) owls hunted unselectively
(i.e., randomly) within the small mammal community; (2)
the collected pellets are a representative sample of the
owls’ catch. Accordingly to the limitations known for these
studies (see Introduction), we limit our inferences from owl
pellets only to the assemblage of species preyed by owls
and their related community without implications on their
true proportion in the community.

lute species richness and diversity index show values on
average higher than those reported in similar studies from
Tyrrhenian central Italy, while trophic level index show a
medium value and Microtinae/Murinae ratio a medium–

The values obtained may reflect the wide and hetero-
geneous agro-forest landscape, with a low anthropogenic
impact, represented by the ‘‘Monte Soratte’’ nature reserve.
Reflecting this landscape heterogeneity, the small mammal
assemblage at our study site includes species, which differ
ecologically; among them: (1) thermo-xerophilous species
of high trophic level (shrews), (2) synanthropic species (es,
murinae as Rattus sp. and Mus musculus), and (2) species
linked both to agricultural (e.g., Microtus savii) and for-
ested habitats (Muscardinus avellanarius and Myodes
glareolus).
The locally more abundant species (Microtus savii,
Apodemus sylvaticus, Apodemus flavicollis) are also those
more frequently observed in the agro-forested landscape
mosaics of central Italy (e.g., Amori et al. 2009), confirming
their dominance in these Mediterranean environments.
Abundance/biomass comparisons curves partially over-
lapped and, even though the biomass curve was slightly
higher than the abundance curve (Fig. 1), the difference
was not significant nor the W value different from zero.
Following the general ABC model, this implies that the
small mammal assemblage we studied could be affected by
a low to moderate disturbance (Magurran 2004 and refer-
ence therein). However, it is noteworthy that ABC curves
emphasize the different ecological role that the biomass
and abundance parameters have at the community level. In
particular, the abundance curves indicate a relative distri-
bution of the spatial niche and dominance of the species,
while biomass curves indicate the relative distribution of
the energy flow in the assemblage, according to the trophic
resources used by species (Begon et al. 1986; Krebs 2001).
The abundance/biomass comparisons are based on the
assumption that in disturbed habitats, small-sized species
(i.e., with low body weight, low trophic level and/or
r-selected) tend to increase in their abundance. As conse-
quence, the abundance curves approach an asymptote
before the biomass curves. On the contrary, in undisturbed
habitats the opposite pattern may be observed, with the
biomass curves cumulating before the abundance curves,
an indication that a higher number of large-sized species of
high trophic level occur in a more complex and diverse
assemblage (Magurran 2004). Following this approach,
early cumulating abundance curves may indicate that the
resources are used by few dominant (i.e., more abundant)
species with a broad spatial niche (i.e., generalist), while early
cumulating biomass curves may indicate that the individuals
with high body weight (and species with a high biomass)
largely occur in the assemblage (Magurran 2004). When
abundance and biomass curves are compared, we then may
obtain information on the level of anthropogenic or natural
disturbance that, sensu lato, affects the assemblage by alter-
nating relative dominance patterns among large specialized
species versus small and generalist species.
Following this general model, the pattern we observed
suggests that the small mammal assemblage in our study
area is characterized by a low level of (anthropogenic or
natural) disturbance, as also indicated by diversity and
trophic level indices, as well as by other evidences (e.g.,
the study site is comprised in a nature reserve with low
level of rural and urban anthropization).
Rend. Fis. Acc. Lincei (2012) 23:349–354
According to our findings, we nevertheless believe that
when the ABC model is applied to small mammal assem-
blages, a cautionary interpretation of the results is needed.
In small mammal assemblages, large body species are
herbivorous, often synanthropic (e.g., Rattus sp.) and typ-
ical of disturbed and anthropized habitats, while small body
species are carnivorous (e.g., shrews), in higher trophic
levels and associated to undisturbed habitats (e.g., insec-
tivores are sensitive to a chemical disturbance in agricul-
ture; Amori et al. 2008 and references therein). This pattern
is different compared to the other communities to which
the ABC model was originally applied (i.e., large body
mass species are specialized and of higher trophic level;
Krebs 2001; Magurran 2004). Therefore, in disturbed
habitats the increase in abundance frequency of small
mammal individuals with high body mass (e.g., Rattus sp.)
may correspond to an early cumulating biomass curve that
may be wrongly interpreted in terms of an undisturbed
assemblage. On the contrary, in undisturbed habitats an
increase of frequency of individuals belonging to small
species (i.e., with low body mass) may develop an early
cumulating abundance curve, higher when compared to
biomass curve that may wrongly suggest disturbed
assemblages. Therefore, the pattern hypothesized for ABC
curves (i.e., biomass frequencies early cumulating when
compared to abundance frequencies in undisturbed
assemblages) is probably not universal but limited only to
assemblages where high body mass species coincide to
species of higher trophic level. A cautionary interpretation
of ABC curves has been also suggested for different tax-
onomic groups (invertebrates; Warwick and Clarke 1994).
Small mammal assemblages obtained indirectly by
owl’s pellets may be considered ‘‘opportunistic’’ assem-
blages where we assume that the relative frequencies in
abundance (and biomass) are proportional to the true
abundance. As stated previously, this assumption is weak
and difficult to test (Capizzi and Luiselli 1996; Yom-Tov
and Wool 1997). Therefore, although small mammal
studies by pellets may be useful to obtain first and indirect
information on autecology, biogeography and environ-
mental management, analyses that foresee the use and
comparisons of single species abundance may induce
incorrect conclusions (e.g., in ABC approaches). Further
research, such as comparing pellet-derived assemblages
from undisturbed and disturbed sites, should be carried out
to verify our cautionary interpretation.
